hints: Fix one person and decide who they shake hands with. What must be true about the number of people on each side of that handshake?
A non-crossing handshake divides the remaining people into two independent smaller circles/intervals.
Define dp[p] as the number of valid configurations for p people and combine the two resulting subproblems for every possible partner.
The resulting sequence is the Catalan sequence; apply modulo 10^9 + 7 throughout the computation.
title: Handshakes That Don't Cross Problem

notes: The input always satisfies the documented constraints.
The answer is the Catalan number C_(numPeople/2) modulo 10^9 + 7.
constraints: numPeople represents people standing around a circle, with each person participating in exactly one handshake.
Return the number of non-crossing handshake configurations modulo 10^9 + 7.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array containing one integer argument, e.g. [4]
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialised integer return value

sampleTestCases.explanation: With two people there is exactly one handshake, so there is one valid non-crossing arrangement.
There are two non-crossing perfect matchings around the circle: adjacent pairs (1,2),(3,4), or (2,3),(4,1).
There are five distinct ways to pair six people around the circle without any handshake chords crossing.
For eight people the count is the fourth Catalan number, 14.

content.problemStatement:
You are given an even number of people `numPeople` that stand around a circle and each person shakes hands with someone else so that there are `numPeople / 2` handshakes total.

Return *the number of ways these handshakes could occur such that none of the handshakes cross*.

Since the answer could be very large, return it **modulo** `10^9 + 7`.

notes: All supported implementations use O(numPeople^2) time and O(numPeople) auxiliary space.
The maximum valid input is 1000, so a static DP allocation is sufficient in C.
Only even-sized subproblems are reachable from the recurrence.
Use a wide integer type for the product before applying the modulus in C, C++, and Java.
The recurrence counts each non-crossing perfect matching exactly once by the partner chosen for the first person.
solution.approach: Let dp[p] be the number of valid non-crossing handshake configurations for p people, with dp[0] = 1. Fix the first person and pair them with each valid odd-indexed partner. That handshake splits the circle into two independent even-sized groups, so each split contributes dp[left] * dp[right]. Summing these contributions gives the Catalan recurrence, and every update is reduced modulo 10^9 + 7.

better.complexity: O(numPeople^2) time and O(numPeople) memoization space.
better.description: Use memoized recursion. For a group of p people, pair a fixed first person with each allowable partner. The chosen handshake splits the remaining people into two independent even-sized groups, so memoization reuses the results of those subproblems.

optimal.complexity: O(numPeople^2) time and O(numPeople) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: Build the same Catalan recurrence bottom-up. For each even p, pair the first person with each odd-indexed partner and add dp[left] * dp[right]. Taking the modulus during each update keeps all stored values bounded.

bruteForce.complexity: Super-exponential/factorial-scale enumeration; not suitable for the constraints.
bruteForce.description: Enumerate all perfect pairings of the people around the circle and reject any pairing containing crossing handshake chords. The number of pairings grows factorially, so this is practical only for very small inputs.

followUps: Can you derive the Catalan closed form from the recurrence?
Can you implement the recurrence with memoization instead of bottom-up dynamic programming?
What changes if the number of people is allowed to be odd or zero as an input contract?

learningObjectives: Recognize non-crossing pairing problems as Catalan-number structures.
Derive a dynamic-programming recurrence from a divide-and-conquer decomposition.
Apply modular arithmetic safely when intermediate counts grow rapidly.
Translate a recurrence into iterative implementations across multiple programming languages.
